summary:
Malacca is one of the thirteen states of Malaysia and stands under the national criminal framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", which covers oral and anal sex for any person regardless of gender, consent or privacy, with a maximum of twenty years' imprisonment and whipping. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. These provisions are not confined to Malaysian citizens and are applied to foreign nationals, so a visitor to Malacca who is neither a citizen nor a Muslim is exposed to federal charges alone. The Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile, last updated in 2024, records these sections together with section 377D, "outrages on decency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years that the profile describes as usable to target transgender people.

Section 377D remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but the Human Dignity Trust records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years and a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, so the low rate of use is a pattern of restraint rather than a legal protection.

A second layer applies in Malacca through the state Sharia enactment. Every one of Malaysia's thirteen states maintains an offence criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", alongside the offences of liwat and musahaqah, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences reach Muslims only; non-Muslim visitors fall under the Federal Penal Code. The enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers of the state Islamic religious department on the ground.

An HRW report published on 10 August 2022, produced with Justice for Sisters, documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia. It cites the federal penal code's twenty-year maximum for oral and anal sex, the Sharia codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, conversion and rehabilitation programmes, and officials shutting down events. Its conclusion is that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behaviour and public discourse, which describes the environment a transgender visitor enters in Malacca as much as anywhere else in the country.

Arbitrary arrest of transgender people is documented across decades and includes repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times, a mass arrest of sixteen trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention. In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists demanded that the order be revoked.

Criminal exposure extends to social venues. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were published; seventeen civil servants identified among the arrestees were suspended. A magistrate rejected the request to extend remand on the ground that no case had been made out under 377B, yet release was delayed and more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including thirty-one foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited, and within days police raided another sauna in Penang. Earlier venue raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and eleven shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches.

Violence against transgender women is lethal and largely unpunished. A trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months. The Human Dignity Trust reports consistent discrimination and violence, with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse, and records a high-profile 2021 case in which a prominent transgender woman fled the country following threats of arrest.

Identity documents remain under state control. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes, and a 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and is unaffected by reassignment surgery. The edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical, in 1975, when the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

No explicit visa rule addresses transgender visitors. The nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay, together with a warning to gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable, no political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform, and Mahathir told the Cambridge Union in June 2019 that Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage.

Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Custodial and institutional alternatives to prison sit in the same Sharia enactments: sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and may order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states, extended to a year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

The framework has survived challenge. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, in each case on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence rather than on the substance, and nothing under the Federal Penal Code was decriminalised.
tangentialFactors:
The national climate has hardened since the 2018 election, which the Human Dignity Trust treats as the start of a documented crackdown on the LGBT community, and the August 2022 HRW and Justice for Sisters findings extend that assessment through conversion and rehabilitation programmes, event shutdowns and the influence of official antipathy on judicial outcomes. A visitor to Malacca therefore arrives in a jurisdiction whose enforcement temperature is set nationally and can change quickly, as the November and December 2025 sauna raids show.

Courts have been willing to remove Sharia cross-dressing provisions, but only on federalism grounds about legislative competence. The Federal Court's February 2021 decision on Selangor and its February 2024 decision on sixteen Kelantan provisions left the substance of the offences undisturbed wherever the enacting legislature was competent, and the Federal Penal Code was untouched by either ruling. The outcome of a challenge therefore turns on who enacted the provision rather than on whether it is compatible with rights.

Malaysia's states are treated as a single pattern rather than as separate regimes for this purpose: all thirteen maintain cross-dressing offences with the same headline penalties of three years, RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, while the degree of institutional alternatives to prison varies, with Terengganu's 2022 amendment extending rehabilitation orders to a year where other states stop at six months. Malacca's own provision sits inside that range, not apart from it.

The 2021 prosecution of the transgender woman Nur Sajat in Selangor, and her flight from the country following threats of arrest, is the clearest illustration of how a case arising in one state can end in exile, a trajectory that does not depend on where in Malaysia the proceedings begin.
localsOnly:
Residents of Malacca who are Muslim face the state Sharia enactment in addition to the Federal Penal Code, and the two layers are handled by different institutions: the state Islamic religious department enforces the cross-dressing, liwat and musahaqah offences, while the police act under sections 377A, 377B and 377D. Non-Muslim residents are subject only to the Federal Penal Code.

Because the Sharia enactments carry no legal definition of transgender dress, residents' day-to-day presentation is judged by officers rather than by a statutory standard, and the documented pattern of repeated arrests of the same individuals, strip-searches and sexual assault in detention falls on this population.

The 1982 fatwa that sex is fixed at birth is applied in practice to residents despite never having been gazetted, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. There is no avenue in Malaysian law for a resident to obtain a corrected gender marker: Registration Department refusals are routine and the single 2016 High Court order requiring an update was overturned on appeal in 2017.

Where a sharia court does convict, it may impose an approved home for up to six months for musahaqah or a counselling or rehabilitation order in a religious institution, so a conviction can end in institutional confinement rather than prison. There is no statutory protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation for residents to invoke, and no political party currently pursues LGBTQ legal reform.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any arrest under the Malacca Sharia cross-dressing provision, or any police action under sections 377A to 377D, has been recorded in Malacca specifically is unresolved here: the inventory supplies national and other-state enforcement examples, including the June 2014 mass arrest and the November 2025 Chow Kit raid, and no Malacca-specific case.

The wording and current penalties of Malacca's own Sharia enactment as amended are not sourced in this inventory; the three-year, RM5,000 and six-stroke figures are the general range recorded across the thirteen states, and whether Malacca has adopted an amendment comparable to Terengganu's 2022 change is not stated.

Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 statement that the section 377 provisions would be revisited has produced any legislative change is not sourced here, and no outcome of that review is recorded.

The current practice of the authorities at Malacca's point of entry regarding gender markers on foreign passports is not sourced. The inventory records no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors, and the 2001 statement on deporting gay foreign officials is the nearest documented entry-policy declaration; whether it reflects present-day admissibility practice is unresolved.

The Human Dignity Trust's statement that the law has been enforced in recent years is not broken down by state, so which states accounted for those prosecutions is unresolved.
